title: Manage application secrets with Azure Key Vault

questions.q: A RAG API's managed identity needs to read an Azure OpenAI key from Key Vault at runtime, and nothing else. Which role should it get?

options.why: Reader sees metadata but not secret values.
Contributor is control plane only and can't read secrets.
Officer can create and delete secrets, more than needed.
Correct. Read-only access to secret values for application identities.

questions.hint: Read secret values and nothing else: the narrowest data-plane secrets role.
questions.explain: Least privilege: apps read with Secrets User; pipelines manage with Secrets Officer.

questions.q: What is the maximum size of a Key Vault secret value?

options.why: Learn gives a smaller limit.
Correct. Secrets store strings up to 25 KB.
256 KB is the Service Bus Standard message limit.
Learn gives a larger limit.

questions.hint: Key Vault secrets have a fixed size limit in kilobytes.
questions.explain: Secrets are opaque strings up to 25 KB with an optional content_type.

questions.q: Compliance requires that encryption keys be protected by FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware security modules. Which tier do you need?

options.why: Standard uses software protection validated to FIPS 140 Level 1.
Learn describes Standard and Premium only.
Correct. Premium protects keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs.
Learn describes Standard and Premium only.

questions.hint: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 means hardware security modules.
questions.explain: Choose Premium when regulations mandate HSM-protected keys.

questions.q: A pipeline must encrypt training data and sign model artifacts without the key material ever leaving the vault. Which object type should you use?

options.why: Secrets return their value to the caller.
Correct. Keys perform cryptographic operations server-side.
Certificates manage X.509 lifecycles; the need here is raw crypto operations.
Tags are metadata, not credentials.

questions.hint: Encrypting and signing inside the vault uses one object type.
questions.explain: Secrets for strings, keys for cryptography, certificates for TLS.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A production vault is created with default settings.

rows.text: Soft delete can be turned off later to save storage.
rows.why: Soft delete is on by default and can't be disabled.

rows.text: The soft-delete retention period can be shortened after creation.
rows.why: Retention is set at creation and can't be changed.
Purge protection is optional; consider enabling it on production vaults.

rows.text: A deleted secret can be recovered within the retention period.
rows.why: Soft-deleted objects are recoverable during retention.

questions.hint: Soft delete is on and can't be turned off. Purge protection is optional.
questions.explain: Soft delete (7–90 days, default 90) plus optional purge protection.

questions.q: A vault was accidentally deleted and then recovered from soft delete. Apps now get authorization errors, and rotation events stopped. Why?

options.text: Recovered vaults start with purge protection disabled
options.why: Purge protection isn't the cause of these errors.

options.text: Secrets are given new names after a vault recovery
options.why: Names don't change.

options.text: Recovery restores keys but leaves the secrets out
options.why: Recovery restores the vault's objects.

options.text: Role assignments and Event Grid subscriptions aren't restored
options.why: Correct. They're deleted with the vault and must be recreated manually.

questions.hint: Recovering a vault doesn't bring back everything that pointed at it.
questions.explain: After recovering a vault, recreate its role assignments and Event Grid subscriptions.

questions.q: A platform engineer has Key Vault Contributor on a vault and can create and update it, but gets authorization errors when reading a secret value. Why?

options.text: The vault must be on the Premium tier for users to read secrets
options.why: Tier controls key protection. It doesn't decide who can read secrets.

options.text: Contributor is a control-plane role with no data-plane access
options.why: Correct. Managing the vault resource and reading its secrets are separate permissions.

options.text: Secrets are readable by managed identities, not by user accounts
options.why: Users and pipelines can read secrets with the right data-plane role.

options.text: Contributor can read secrets only after soft delete is turned off
options.why: Soft delete can't be turned off, and it isn't related to read access.

questions.hint: Azure separates managing a resource from using the data inside it.
questions.explain: Key Vault Contributor is a control-plane role: it manages the vault resource but doesn't grant data-plane operations such as reading secrets. Use data-plane roles such as Key Vault Secrets User or Secrets Officer.

questions.q: A monitoring tool must check which secrets exist in a vault and read their properties, such as expiry dates, but must never see secret values. Which role fits?

options.why: Secrets Officer can create, update and delete secrets, which is far more than needed.
Secrets User can read secret values, which this tool must not do.
Correct. It grants read access to vault metadata, such as secret names and properties, without revealing values.
Administrator grants all data-plane operations on keys, secrets and certificates.

questions.hint: You want names and properties, but no values.
questions.explain: Key Vault Reader reads vault metadata (names, properties) without values. Secrets User reads values; Secrets Officer manages secrets; Administrator has all data-plane operations; Contributor is control-plane only.

questions.q: A CI/CD pipeline creates, updates and deletes secrets as part of credential rotation. Which built-in role should its identity get?

options.why: Contributor manages the vault resource, not the secrets inside it.
Reader sees metadata only.
Secrets User is read-only, so the pipeline couldn't create new versions.
Correct. It grants full management of secrets for operators and pipelines that manage the secret lifecycle.

questions.hint: The pipeline manages the lifecycle of secrets, not the vault itself.
questions.explain: Assign Key Vault Secrets Officer to operators or CI/CD pipelines responsible for secret lifecycle; Key Vault Secrets User to apps that only read credentials.

questions.q: At startup, a service must confirm that five required secrets exist without reading their values. Which method should it call?

options.why: That retrieves the values themselves.
That lists versions of one secret.
Correct. It returns metadata such as name and enabled status, not values.
Writing secrets would overwrite them.

questions.hint: One method lists secrets and their properties without returning values.
questions.explain: Validate configuration early by listing secret properties.

questions.q: Which URL format does a SecretClient use for a vault named kv-ragpipeline-prod?

options.why: Correct. Vault URLs follow https://<vault-name>.vault.azure.net/.
The vault name is a subdomain, not a path.
That's an App Service domain.
That isn't the Key Vault domain.

questions.hint: Each vault has its own DNS name under vault.azure.net.
questions.explain: Find it on the vault's overview page or with az keyvault show --query properties.vaultUri.

questions.q: Match each exception to the right response.

items.why: The secret name doesn't exist in the vault.
HttpResponseError covers authentication and authorization failures.
Network-level problems may resolve on retry.

questions.hint: Missing secret, missing permission, or a network problem: each needs a different response.
questions.explain: Distinguish configuration errors from transient network failures.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A FastAPI service on Container Apps uses DefaultAzureCredential with a SecretClient.

rows.text: In Azure, ManagedIdentityCredential authenticates the app without stored credentials.
rows.why: Managed identity is the recommended method on Azure compute.

rows.text: The service should create a new SecretClient for every request.
rows.why: Create it once at startup and reuse it.

rows.text: It's fine to log secret.value for debugging.
rows.why: Log the name and version, not the value.

questions.hint: Managed identity in Azure. Reuse the client. Never log values.
questions.explain: One reusable client, managed identity, no secret values in logs.

questions.q: On a developer laptop, AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID and AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET are set from an old test, and the developer is also signed in with az login. Which credential does DefaultAzureCredential use first?

options.why: Correct. EnvironmentCredential is first in the chain and wins if the variables are set.
Azure CLI comes later in the chain.
There's no managed identity on a laptop, and it comes after Environment.
PowerShell is last.

questions.hint: DefaultAzureCredential tries credentials in a fixed order. Environment variables come early.
questions.explain: The chain tries Environment, Workload Identity, Managed Identity, then CLI, azd and PowerShell.

questions.q: A FastAPI app uses the async SecretClient with an async DefaultAzureCredential. During shutdown, the logs warn about unclosed sessions. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Ignore the warning, because Python closes sessions on exit
options.why: Unclosed sessions can leak resources. Close them explicitly.

options.text: Switch to the synchronous client, which never needs closing
options.why: Learn's guidance for async apps is to close the async client and credential.

options.text: Close both the client and the credential, for example with async with or await close()
options.why: Correct. Both are async context managers that should be closed when you're done.

options.text: Create a new client per request so that nothing stays open
options.why: Reusing one client is the recommendation. Per-request clients add overhead.

questions.hint: Both async objects hold network resources that need to be released.
questions.explain: The async SecretClient and credential are async context managers. Use async with, or call await client.close() and await credential.close(), for example in the app's shutdown hook.

questions.q: How many days before a secret's expiration does the SecretNearExpiry event fire?

options.why: Correct. It fires thirty days before expiration.
Learn gives a longer window.
Learn gives 30.
90 is a typical expiry length, not the warning window.

questions.hint: Key Vault gives a warning window before a secret expires.
questions.explain: Combine a 90-day expiry with SecretNearExpiry for a 30-day rotation window.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A secret named cosmosdb-connection-string has an expires_on date that passed yesterday.

rows.text: get_secret() now fails because the secret expired.
rows.why: Expiration is informational; expired secrets can still be retrieved.

rows.text: Calling set_secret() with the same name overwrites the old value in place.
get_secret() without a version returns the latest enabled version.
rows.why: The default is the latest enabled version.

rows.text: Disabling an old version stops apps retrieving it, even by version ID.
rows.why: enabled=False prevents retrieval of that version.

questions.hint: Expiry doesn't stop reads. Writing the same name creates a new version.
questions.explain: Versions accumulate; expiry signals staleness but doesn't block reads.

questions.q: Rotate a Cosmos DB key with the dual-credential approach. Put the steps in order.
steps: Generate a new secondary key on the service
Store the new key as a new secret version in Key Vault
Wait until every app instance uses the new value
Regenerate the old primary key on the service
questions.hint: Two keys: switch to the new one everywhere before regenerating the old one.
questions.explain: At least one valid credential exists throughout the rotation.

questions.q: After a key rotation, some instances still use the old key and get 401s from the downstream service. What does Learn recommend in application code?

options.text: Call get_secret() before each downstream request
options.why: That floods Key Vault and risks throttling.

options.text: Pin the secret version in the app configuration
options.why: Pinning prevents picking up the rotated version.

options.text: Restart the app instances on a schedule
options.why: Restarts don't target the failure and still leave gaps.

options.text: On auth failure, refetch the secret and retry
options.why: Correct. One extra Key Vault call only when the credential is rejected.

questions.hint: When the downstream service rejects the key, try the latest secret once more.
questions.explain: Retry-on-auth-failure gives zero-downtime rotation without coordination.

questions.q: You want rotation without human steps for an API key that expires every 90 days. What should you set up?

options.text: Purge protection with a 30-day retention period
options.why: Purge protection prevents deletion; it doesn't rotate.

options.text: A monthly calendar reminder for the operations team
options.why: That's manual rotation.
Correct. The handler generates the credential and stores it as a new version.

options.text: A second vault that mirrors the first one's secrets
options.why: Mirroring doesn't rotate anything.

questions.hint: An expiry event can start code that creates the new version.
questions.explain: Automated rotation: SecretNearExpiry → Event Grid → Function → new secret version.

questions.q: All app instances now use the newly rotated database credential. You want to make sure nothing can keep using the previous version. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Purge the old version from soft delete
options.why: Versions aren't purged individually. You disable them.

options.text: Set a new tag on the secret named version=old
options.why: Tags are metadata, so they don't stop anyone reading a version.

options.text: Disable the previous version with update_secret_properties(enabled=False)
options.why: Correct. A disabled version can't be retrieved, which enforces use of the new credential.

options.text: Delete the whole secret and recreate it
options.why: That removes every version, including the current one, and breaks the apps.

questions.hint: Old versions stay readable until you change one of their properties.
questions.explain: After a successful rotation, consider disabling previous versions with update_secret_properties(..., enabled=False) so no instance can keep using the old credential. list_properties_of_secret_versions() helps audit versions.

questions.q: An inference API calls get_secret() on every request and starts receiving HTTP 429 during spikes. What's the main fix?

options.text: Cache the secret in memory with a TTL
options.why: Correct. Caching turns thousands of vault calls into a few refreshes.

options.text: Move the vault to the Premium tier
options.why: Tier doesn't raise these throttling limits.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; immediate retries make it worse.

options.text: Create a new SecretClient per request
options.why: New clients add overhead and don't reduce calls.

questions.hint: Calling the vault on every request causes throttling. Keep secrets for a short while.
questions.explain: Key Vault allows up to 4,000 GETs per vault per 10 seconds.

questions.q: Which Key Vault event should an app subscribe to so it can invalidate its cache as soon as a secret is rotated?

options.why: That fires after expiry passes.
That fires 30 days before expiry, used to trigger rotation.
Correct. It fires when a new secret version is stored.
That's a Blob Storage event.

questions.hint: A new version means rotation. Which event announces it?
questions.explain: Combine event-driven invalidation with a time-based fallback.

questions.q: An API key rotates every week, and the team needs fresh credentials soon after rotation. Which cache setup fits Learn's guidance?

options.text: No cache; call Key Vault on each request
options.why: Uncached reads risk throttling.
Correct. High-rotation secrets need short TTLs and Event Grid.
That's for monthly or quarterly rotation.

options.text: Startup preload refreshed every few hours
options.why: That's for annual or static secrets.

questions.hint: A short TTL, with events to invalidate early.
questions.explain: Match cache lifetime to rotation frequency and revocation risk.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team considers caching secrets in a shared Azure Managed Redis instance for 50 replicas.

rows.text: It can cut Key Vault calls to one per refresh cycle regardless of replica count.
rows.why: One process fetches; others read the shared cache.

rows.text: It adds no new security considerations, because Redis is inside Azure.
rows.why: Secrets now live in another place needing access control and encryption.

rows.text: Per-process caching makes Key Vault calls independent of the number of instances.
rows.why: Per-process calls scale linearly with instances; a shared cache makes them independent.

rows.text: Retrying 429s should use exponential backoff with random jitter.

questions.hint: A shared cache cuts calls but adds its own risks.
questions.explain: Shared caches reduce calls but add complexity and exposure.
